extracted.intended_audience: researchers, mathematicians, journal editors, and readers interested in scholarly publishing and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative considerations and practices surrounding a journal's decision to withdraw or correct a mathematical research paper, including proofs' correctness, editorial handling, and post-publication remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof completeness and correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper was retracted because the proofs in the paper were found to be incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Errors/gaps in proofs—here, two proofs—are substantive defects that can justify withdrawal; gaps may be discovered later when others try to use the techniques. Example from the page: a gap was found by other mathematicians using the techniques, prompting the author to prepare corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author remediation via erratum/corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may submit errata or corrected arguments to address identified errors (author sent a one-page erratum in 2008, expanded to two pages after referee feedback, and later sent a four-page version replacing a lemma in 2015).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting progressively detailed corrections and replacement arguments is an appropriate remediation path; these should be evaluated by editors/referees. The presence of an erratum can be a reason to correct rather than retract, provided the corrections adequately fix the issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial assessment: correction versus retraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors must decide whether to correct a paper or withdraw it; in this case the journal intended to withdraw the paper rather than publish the author's corrections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community views (as cited) suggest retraction is appropriate if the original research is unreliable or would require numerous/cumulative corrections ('mega correction'); conversely, if errors are fixable with a clear erratum, correction may be preferable. The decision should weigh reliability of the published record and the feasibility of a trustworthy correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and communication from editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors expect to receive referee reports and clear communication about the status of submitted corrections; the author asked several times for the referee reports and heard nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good editorial practice includes timely acknowledgement, sharing referee feedback, and clear explanations of decisions. Anti-patterns: long silence, failure to provide referee reports, and abrupt withdrawal decisions without explaining reasoning to the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of handling errata and corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant delays occurred: initial communication about a gap was in 2008, further corrections were sent in 2015, and the author heard nothing for over a year before the 2017 withdrawal notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially in highly technical/small expert communities, prompt handling of errata is important. Long delays impede resolution and can lead to confusion about whether correction or retraction is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer scrutiny and post-publication verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Gaps in the paper were found when other mathematicians tried to use the paper's techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical use and scrutiny by peers can reveal flaws not caught in initial review; post-publication engagement is an important mechanism for detecting errors and assessing the reliability of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and content of retraction/withdrawal notices
rubrics_metrics.description: The retraction notice here simply states the paper 'is hereby withdrawn.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction notices that are minimal provide little information to readers; clearer notices explaining the reason (e.g., incomplete proofs) help the community understand the nature and severity of the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for corrected work to be republished or posted
rubrics_metrics.description: The retraction 'does not preclude the author from publishing a correct manuscript when and if they figure it out'; the author plans to post his correction on arXiv.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when a paper is withdrawn, authors can remedy the record by preparing corrected versions and making them publicly available (e.g., on preprint servers) or resubmitting to journals; retraction is not necessarily an absolute end to dissemination of corrected results.
